questions.stem:
A vertical tube is completely filled with water. A small sound source of constant frequency is held slightly above the open upper end. Water runs out from the lower end and a number of resonance positions are detected. The first of these occurs when the water surface is 15 cm below the top of the tube and the next occurs at 49 cm. The speed of sound in air as 330 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

What is the frequency of the source?
questions.stemText: A vertical tube is completely filled with water. A small sound source of constant frequency is held slightly above the open upper end. Water runs out from the lower end and a number of resonance positions are detected. The first of these occurs when the water surface is 15 cm below the top of the tube and the next occurs at 49 cm. The speed of sound in air as 330 m s−1. What is the frequency of the source? A 390 Hz B 490 Hz C 500 Hz D 550 Hz

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer the wavelength from the spacing of successive resonances.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the open-end correction

explanation.body: Consecutive resonant lengths differ by half a wavelength, so $\lambda/2=0.49-0.15=0.34\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\lambda=0.68\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $v=f\lambda$ gives $330=f(0.68)$ and hence $f=490\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Implies an 85 cm wavelength, larger than twice the measured resonance spacing.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Rounds the calculated frequency too coarsely.
perOption.D: Treats the first 15 cm length as exactly one quarter wavelength.

In a Young’s double slit experiment, a red light from a laser is incident on the source slit $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{o}}$ and passes through the double slits $\mathrm{S}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{S}_{2}$, producing red bright fringes as shown the figure below.

Subsequently, a transparent thin glass block is placed in front of $\mathrm{S}_{1}$.

Which observation is correct?

Subsequently, a transparent thin glass block is placed in front of S1. S1 red light source (laser) central line So S2 Which observation is correct? A The fringe separation will decrease. B The fringe separation will be non-uniform. C The contrast between bright and dark fringes will increase. D The central maximum will be shifted upwards.

options.label: B
options.text: The fringe separation will be non-uniform.

options.label: C
options.text: The contrast between bright and dark fringes will increase.

options.label: D
options.text: The central maximum will be shifted upwards.

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must connect the added phase delay to the direction of the fringe shift.
questions.misconception: Confusing fringe shift with fringe spacing

explanation.body: Glass has a higher refractive index than air, so the light travels more slowly and has a shorter wavelength inside the glass. The block therefore contains more wavelengths than the same thickness of air. The central maximum shifts upwards, where the shorter geometric path from $S_1$ compensates for the extra phase delay.

perOption.A: Uses the wavelength in glass to predict the fringe spacing on the screen.
perOption.B: Treats the delay from the thin glass block as varying from fringe to fringe.
perOption.C: Confuses the phase delay with an improvement in the balance of the two beam intensities.
perOption.D: Correct.

What is the total number of intensity maxima from the grating that can be observed?

A 3
B 4

questions.difficultyReason: The grating equation gives the order limit, which must be converted into a count on both sides.
questions.misconception: Rounding the maximum order up

perOption.B: Counts the central maximum and the orders on just one side.

questions.stemText:
The angular resolution of a vertical slit for a pair of objects is $4.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

What is the new angular resolution if the width of the slit is doubled?

A $1.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$
B $2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$
C $8.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$
D $16\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The Rayleigh criterion gives an immediate inverse-proportion calculation.
questions.misconception: Assuming angular resolution increases with slit width

explanation.body: By Rayleigh’s criterion, $\theta\approx\lambda/b$. Doubling the slit width gives $\theta_{\mathrm{new}}/\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=b_{\mathrm{old}}/b_{\mathrm{new}}=0.5$. The new angular resolution is $2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Assumes inverse-square dependence on slit width.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes direct rather than inverse proportionality.
perOption.D: Assumes angular resolution grows as the square of slit width.

questions.misconception: Inverting the diffraction angle

explanation.body: The limiting angle is $\theta\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the dish diameter. By the small-angle approximation, $x/D\approx\theta$, so $x=\lambda D/b=(0.40\times10^{-6})(2.8\times10^{25})/5.1=2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must locate the first node from an antinode before counting the remaining nodes.
questions.misconception: Counting nodes from the wrong starting phase

explanation.body: The receiver travels $33.5/12.0=2.79$ wavelengths. Since X is an antinode, the nodes occur $0.25\lambda$, $0.75\lambda$, $1.25\lambda$, $1.75\lambda$, $2.25\lambda$ and $2.75\lambda$ from X, so six minima are detected.

perOption.A: Counts only complete wavelengths, missing the nodes spaced half a wavelength apart.
perOption.B: Counting just the nodes at quarter-wavelength plus whole-wavelength offsets skips every second node.
perOption.C: Counting only complete half-wavelength intervals misses the sixth node at $2.75\lambda$.

questions.stem:
Monochromatic light is incident normally on a single slit. The resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen. The width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is x.

The distance between the single slit and the screen is much greater than the slit width and is unchanged.

The light source is replaced by another light source of light with twice the wavelength, and the single slit is replaced by one that has half the slit width.

What is the linear width of the new central maximum in terms of x?
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a single slit. The resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen. The width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is x. The distance between the single slit and the screen is much greater than the slit width and is unchanged. The light source is replaced by another light source of light with twice the wavelength, and the single slit is replaced by one that has half the slit width. What is the linear width of the new central maximum in terms of x? A 0.5x B x C 2x D 4x

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Small-angle single-slit relation with two simultaneous factor changes.
questions.misconception: Thinking the two changes cancel

explanation.body:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$. Since the slit-screen distance $D$ is much greater than the slit width, the angle is small.

$\theta = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}x}{D} = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so $x = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{b}$.

New width: $x' = \dfrac{2(2\lambda)D}{b/2} = \dfrac{8\lambda D}{b} = 4x$.

perOption.A: Wrong proportionality; $x \propto \lambda/b$, so both changes widen the pattern.
perOption.B: Assumes the two changes cancel, but doubling λ and halving b both increase the width.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two changes.
perOption.D: Correct.

(angles of diffraction; intensities) A $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$; same B $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$; second order dimmer C $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$; same D $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$; second order dimmer

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that sin θ, not θ, scales with order, and recalling that higher orders are dimmer.
questions.misconception: Assuming $\theta \propto n$ rather than $\sin\theta \propto n$

explanation.body:
$\sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{(1)\lambda}{d}$ and $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{(2)\lambda}{d}$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$.

The rate of increase of $\sin\theta$ decreases as $\theta$ increases from 0 to 90°, so $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$.

At higher orders, since the distance travelled by the light increases, intensity decreases, so the second order is dimmer.

perOption.A: Assumes $\theta \propto n$, but it is $\sin\theta$ that is proportional to $n$; also intensity is not the same.
perOption.B: Assumes $\theta \propto n$; it is $\sin\theta$ that doubles.
perOption.C: Angle relation is right, but higher orders are dimmer.

questions.misconception: Unit/power-of-ten errors with km and nm

questions.stemText:
In a double-slit interference experiment, one slit transmits waves of twice the amplitude compared to the other slit. The intensity at one of the bright fringes on the screen is $I_o$.

What is the intensity at the dark fringe closest to this bright fringe?

A zero
B $I_o/2$
C $I_o/4$
D $I_o/9$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: In a double-slit interference experiment, one slit transmits waves of twice the amplitude compared to the other slit. The intensity at one of the bright fringes

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine unequal amplitudes before squaring their ratio.
questions.misconception: Assuming all destructive interference gives zero intensity

explanation.body: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. The bright fringe has $I_o\propto(2A+A)^2$ and the dark fringe has $I\propto(2A-A)^2$. Thus $I/I_o=(A/3A)^2=1/9$.

perOption.A: Complete cancellation requires equal amplitudes.
perOption.B: The factor of two compares the individual slit amplitudes and gives no fringe intensity ratio.
perOption.C: This squares the ratio of the individual slit amplitudes in place of the resultant amplitudes.
perOption.D: Correct. The dark-fringe intensity is one ninth of the bright-fringe intensity.

questions.stemText:

The observer views the panels with a telescope that has an aperture diameter of 200 mm. Assume that the panels act as point sources of light for the observer.

Which of the following is correct?

Will the two images seen by the observer be resolved? | Angular separation of two panels as measured from aperture / rad
A Yes | $2.5\times10^{-6}$
B Yes | $7.5\times10^{-5}$

questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate the observed angle and compare it with the diffraction limit.
questions.misconception: Confusing angular separation with the resolution limit

explanation.body: Using $s=r\theta$, the angular separation is $\theta=25/(335\times10^3)=7.46\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$, or $7.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$. questions.misconception: Judging diffraction by slit width alone.

questions.stem:
A diffraction grating with 500 lines per mm is used to observe diffraction of monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm.

The light is passed through a narrow slit and the grating is placed so that its lines are parallel to the slit. Light passes through the slit and then the grating.

An observer views the slit through the grating at different angles, moving his head from X parallel to the grating, through Y, opposite the slit, to Z parallel to the grating on the opposite side.

How many images of the slit does he see?
questions.stemText: A diffraction grating with 500 lines per mm is used to observe diffraction of monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm. The light is passed through a narrow slit and the grating is placed so that its lines are parallel to the slit. Light passes through the slit and then the grating. An observer views the slit through the grating at different angles, moving his head from X parallel to the grating, through Y, opposite the slit, to Z parallel to the grating on the opposite side. How many images of the slit does he see? A 3 B 4 C 6 D 7

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires finding the grating spacing, taking the highest integer order and counting both sides.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the central maximum or one side of the pattern.

explanation.body: The grating spacing is $d=\frac{1.0\times10^{-3}}{500}=2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ with $\sin\theta=1$ gives $n=\frac{2.0\times10^{-6}}{600\times10^{-9}}=3.33$, so the highest actual order is 3 on each side. Including the central maximum gives $3+3+1=7$ images.

perOption.A: Counts only the three noncentral orders on one side.
perOption.B: Counts the central image and the three orders on one side only.
perOption.C: Counts both sides but omits the central image.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem:
Monochromatic light is incident on a pair of narrow slits a distance of 0.1 mm apart. A series of bright and dark fringes are observed on a screen a distance of 2.0 m away. The distance between adjacent bright fringes is 8.0 mm.

What is the path difference between the light waves from the two slits that meet at the second order dark fringe?
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident on a pair of narrow slits a distance of 0.1 mm apart. A series of bright and dark fringes are observed on a screen a distance of 2.0 m away. The distance between adjacent bright fringes is 8.0 mm. What is the path difference between the light waves from the two slits that meet at the second order dark fringe? A 2.0 × $10^{-7}$ m B 4.0 × $10^{-7}$ m C 6.0 × $10^{-7}$ m D 8.0 × $10^{-7}$ m

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the wavelength and identifying the second destructive-interference condition.
questions.misconception: Using a whole-wavelength path difference for a dark fringe.

explanation.body: From $x=\lambda D/a$, the wavelength is $\lambda=(0.008)(0.0001)/2.0=4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$. The slit sources are in phase, so dark fringes occur at path differences $(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$ with $n=0,1,\dots$. The second dark fringe has $n=1$, so its path difference is $1.5\lambda=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\lambda/2$, which gives the first dark fringe.
perOption.B: Uses $\lambda$, which gives the first bright fringe away from the centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The second dark fringe has a path difference of one and a half wavelengths.
perOption.D: Uses $2\lambda$, which gives the second bright fringe away from the centre.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must halve the angle, find $d/\lambda$ and then count the orders on both sides plus the central maximum.
questions.misconception: Using 56° rather than 28° as the diffraction angle, or forgetting the central maximum

explanation.body:
The second-order lines are $56°$ apart, so each is at $\theta = 28°$: $d\sin 28° = 2\lambda \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°}$.

Number of diffraction lines $= (4 \times 2) + 1 = 9$

perOption.B: Counts only one side of the central maximum, plus the zeroth order.
perOption.C: Counts both sides but leaves out the zeroth-order (central) line.
perOption.D: Correct. $n_{\max} = 4$ on each side, plus the central maximum.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must choose a visible wavelength themselves and combine the Rayleigh criterion with the small-angle approximation.

explanation.body:
Distance $r = 20 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$. By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta \approx \lambda/D$, so the minimum separation is $s = r\theta = r\dfrac{\lambda}{D}$.

Violet (400 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(400 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 2.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Red (700 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(700 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 4.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Across the visible range, the order of magnitude is $10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too small by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $r$ or $\lambda$.
perOption.B: Correct. $s = r\lambda/D \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for visible light.
perOption.C: Too large by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $\lambda$ (for example, using micrometres as nanometres).
perOption.D: Far too large. It does not follow from $s = r\lambda/D$ with visible wavelengths.

perOption.C: This is $s$, the half-width; the central maximum spans from one first minimum to the other.

questions.stem:
The sound from a loudspeaker placed above a tube causes resonance of the air in the tube. A stationary wave is formed with two nodes and two antinodes as shown.

The speed of sound in air is 330 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The frequency of the sound from the loudspeaker is now increased to the next higher resonance of air in the tube. What is the new frequency of the sound?
questions.stemText: The sound from a loudspeaker placed above a tube causes resonance of the air in the tube. A stationary wave is formed with two nodes and two antinodes as shown. The speed of sound in air is 330 m s−1. The frequency of the sound from the loudspeaker is now increased to the next higher resonance of air in the tube. What is the new frequency of the sound? A 138 Hz B 413 Hz C 688 Hz D 963 Hz

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Must identify the current mode from the diagram and know only odd harmonics exist in a closed tube.
questions.misconception: Thinking the next resonance adds a half wavelength rather than stepping to the next odd quarter

explanation.body:
The tube is closed at the bottom (node) and open at the top (antinode). The current pattern is $\frac{3}{4}\lambda$; the next higher resonance is $\frac{5}{4}\lambda$.

$\frac{5}{4}\lambda = 60\ \mathrm{cm} \Rightarrow \lambda = 48\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.48\ \mathrm{m}$

$v = f\lambda$: $330 = f(0.48)$, so $f = 688\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Fundamental ($\frac{1}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm), a lower resonance not a higher one.
perOption.B: The current resonance ($\frac{3}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm), not the next higher one.
perOption.C: Correct. $\frac{5}{4}\lambda = 0.60$ m gives 688 Hz.
perOption.D: Skips a harmonic ($\frac{7}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm).

The intensity of the wave from $S_{1}$ is 4I while the intensity of the wave from $S_{2}$ is I. The waves meet at point P to form a bright fringe due to constructive interference and meet at point Q to form a dark fringe due to destructive interference. What is the ratio of the intensity of light at point P to the intensity of light at point Q?
questions.stemText: Two coherent wave sources, S1 and S2, emit light waves of the same frequency but different intensity. The intensity of the wave from S1 is 4I while the intensity of the wave from S2 is I. The waves meet at point P to form a bright fringe due to constructive interference and meet at point Q to form a dark fringe due to destructive interference. What is the ratio of the intensity of light at point P to the intensity of light at point Q? A 0.11 B 1.7 C 4.0 D 9.0

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting intensities to amplitudes before combining and squaring them.
questions.misconception: Adding or subtracting intensities directly.

explanation.body: Since $I=kA^2$, if the amplitude from $S_2$ is $A$, the amplitude from $S_1$ is $2A$. The resultant amplitude is $2A+A=3A$ at P and $2A-A=A$ at Q. Thus $\frac{I_P}{I_Q}=\frac{(3A)^2}{A^2}=9.0$.

perOption.A: Reverses the bright-to-dark intensity ratio.
perOption.B: Adds and subtracts intensities directly, giving $5/3$.
perOption.C: Uses the source intensity ratio without combining the waves.
perOption.D: Correct.

Light of wavelength 690 nm passes through a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm, producing a series of bright spots (maxima) on a screen.

What is the total number of bright spots that are produced?
questions.stemText: Light of wavelength 690 nm passes through a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm, producing a series of bright spots (maxima) on a screen. What is the total number of bright spots that are produced? A 4 B 8 C 9 D 11

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting line density to spacing, finding the highest integer order and counting both sides.
questions.misconception: Omitting the zero-order maximum.

explanation.body: Use $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\frac{1}{300\times1000}\sin90^\circ=n(690\times10^{-9})$, giving an order limit of about $4.83$. The highest observable integer order is $4$, so there are $4+1+4=9$ bright spots.

perOption.A: Counts the nonzero orders on only one side.
perOption.B: Omits the central maximum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up to five even though the fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.
